questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Who Is a Citizen' refers to.
questions.a: A citizen is a full member of the political community - bound to the country by law and allegiance, enjoying civil, political and social rights, and owing duties in return; citizenship links individual freedom with shared responsibility for the nation.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Who Is a Citizen'.
questions.a: Citizenship is a two-way bond: rights flow to the citizen, duties flow back to the community.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Who Is a Citizen' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 5 (source: hees205.txt lines 5-62 (rights and duties, meaning of citizenship))

concepts.title: Fundamental Rights in the Indian Constitution

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Fundamental Rights in the Indian Constitution' refers to.
questions.a: The Constitution guarantees fundamental rights - equality, freedom, against exploitation, freedom of religion, cultural and educational rights, and constitutional remedies - protected by courts, so no government or person may trample them.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Fundamental Rights in the Indian Constitution'.
questions.a: Six families of fundamental rights, enforceable in court, shield every citizen.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Fundamental Rights in the Indian Constitution' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 5 (source: hees205.txt lines 153-227 (fundamental rights in the Indian Constitution), 421-460 (key articles))

concepts.title: Duties: The True Source of Rights

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Duties: The True Source of Rights' refers to.
questions.a: As the chapter's epigraph says, the true source of rights is duty: fundamental duties - respecting the constitution and flag, protecting the environment, striving for excellence and renouncing practices derogatory to women - are what citizens owe so that everyone's rights can flourish.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Duties: The True Source of Rights'.
questions.a: Rights and duties are two sides of one coin - my duty secures your right.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Duties: The True Source of Rights' taught, and from which source text?

concepts.title: Equality and the Fight Against Discrimination

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Equality and the Fight Against Discrimination' refers to.
questions.a: Discrimination - unfair treatment on grounds of caste, religion, gender or birth - violates the constitutional promise of equality; abolishing untouchability and reserving opportunities for the disadvantaged are constitutional tools to convert formal equality into real equality.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Equality and the Fight Against Discrimination'.
questions.a: The constitution not only bans unfair treatment but actively lifts the historically excluded.
